text: Whole slide imaging (WSI) has become a crucial modality in modern histopathology, enabling the digital conversion of tissue on glass slides into high‐resolution virtual slides with magnifications ranging from 2× to 100×, for the entire tissue section (Higgins 2015; Kumar et al. 2020). Beyond facilitating precise, large‐scale visualization, WSI supports the reconstruction of three‐dimensional (3D) volumes from serial histological sections, providing new opportunities to study the microstructural organization of complex tissues such as the brain, liver, lung, cervix, and breast (Bongaerts et al. 2018; Deutsch et al. 2025; Ghaznavi et al. 2013; Melo et al. 2019; Tong et al. 2019). 3D reconstructions from serial WSI are challenged by structural artifacts introduced during tissue preparation and imaging. Global 3D deformations arise from tissue extraction and processing, including shrinkage due to dehydration and fixation or distortions from mechanical stress and embedding (Al‐Kinani 2024). Sectioning and mounting introduce slice‐specific 2D deformations such as tearing, folding, shearing, and local warping (Al‐Kinani 2024). These morphological alterations are compounded by illumination variability (e.g., vignetting) and misalignment between tiles or serial sections, all of which hinder accurate
title: Improved Post-Processing Framework for Whole Slide Imaging and 3D Reconstruction

text: tearing, folding, shearing, and local warping (Al‐Kinani 2024). These morphological alterations are compounded by illumination variability (e.g., vignetting) and misalignment between tiles or serial sections, all of which hinder accurate spatial correspondence (Al‐Kinani 2024). Accurate quantitative analysis of whole slide images is critical for applications including feature extraction, tissue classification and automated cellular quantification (Hanna et al. 2020). Raw microscopy data exhibits spatial pixel intensity inhomogeneities that can lead to stitching errors, intensity discontinuities, and compromise downstream analysis. To address these artifacts, several image correction methods have been developed, including corrected intensity distributions using regularized energy minimization (CIDRE) (Smith et al. 2015), BaSiC (Background and Shading Correction of Optical Microscopy Images) (Peng et al. 2017), and Vignetted Stitched‐Tile Adjustment using Morphological Adaptive Processing (VISTAmap) (Fung et al. 2025). However, these approaches can present reduced accuracy when few tiles are available or where tile‐specific correction may be required (Coster et al. 2014; Likar et al. 2000; Singh et al. 2014; Smith et al. 2015). For stitching WSI tiles to create a single image, tools such as the ImageStitching Plugin in Fiji

text: 2014; Likar et al. 2000; Singh et al. 2014; Smith et al. 2015). For stitching WSI tiles to create a single image, tools such as the ImageStitching Plugin in Fiji (Preibisch et al. 2009) and, more recently, ASHLAR (Alignment by Simultaneous Harmonization of Layer/Adjacency Registration) (Muhlich et al. 2022) have been developed, with ASHLAR specifically addressing residual misalignment from conventional tile‐stitching approaches (Chalfoun et al. 2017) (Zukić et al. 2021). Histological 3D reconstruction methods have progressed from a simple sequential alignment to a reference section (Kiessling and Pichler 2010), which was prone to cumulative distortions such as the z‐shift effect (Yushkevich, Avants, et al. 2006). Without a global anatomical reference, some brain reconstruction frameworks use a pairwise‐only approach with iterative refinement (Woodward et al. 2018). More advanced frameworks integrate WSI with blockface photographs and 3D anatomical references from modalities such as magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), using affine and nonlinear transformations to achieve anatomically faithful reconstructions (Adler et al. 2014; Amunts et al. 2013; Chakravarty et al. 2006; Choe et al. 2011; Dauguet et al. 2009, 2007). Multimodal strategies such as

text: to achieve anatomically faithful reconstructions (Adler et al. 2014; Amunts et al. 2013; Chakravarty et al. 2006; Choe et al. 2011; Dauguet et al. 2009, 2007). Multimodal strategies such as the Possum Framework (Majka and Wojcik 2016) integrate multiple modalities into a unified spatial system and explicitly identify tissue tears and severe displacements as preprocessing challenges that must be addressed before reconstruction. Deformable registration of serial histological sections is an ill‐posed problem that can be constrained by incorporating information about tissue boundaries to guide the registration. The level‐set method (LSM) is a numerical technique that embeds surface information into a signed distance function, representing surfaces implicitly as level‐sets to capture complex geometric and topological changes. This method has been previously used to embed surface‐based structural information in rigid body reconstruction of a rat brain (Kozinska et al. 1997) and to improve cortical surface alignment in human MRI brain images (Tardif et al. 2015). Motivated by the instability of unconstrained deformable registration in regions with weak anatomical contrast, we leverage LSM to introduce anatomically informed surface constraints that stabilize and guide the deformable alignment of serial histological sections. This study presents an enhanced framework for 3D histological image reconstruction that addresses both tile‐level intensity inconsistencies and section‐level geometric distortions. We first introduce an overlap‐aware illumination correction for WSI that enables tile‐specific refinement while preserving global consistency. We then integrate LSM‐based anatomical constraints into the nonlinear registration stage of the Possum framework, stabilizing deformable alignment and mitigating common histological artifacts. Together, these advances aim to enhance reconstruction robustness and achieve more faithful restoration of native tissue morphology in 3D histological image reconstruction.

text: This study utilized in vivo MRI and histological data from a single adult female common marmoset ( Callithrix jacchus (Linnaeus, 1758)) brain. Scanning was performed on a 3T‐PrismaFit scanner (Siemens, Germany) with a 16‐channel marmoset RF coil (Hori et al. 2018) (Takashima Seisakusho Co./Rogue Research Inc.). A T 1‐weighted anatomical MRI scan was acquired using a magnetization prepared rapidly acquired gradient echo (MPRAGE) sequence with the following parameters: flip angle = 8°, TR = 2200 ms, TI = 706 ms, isotropic resolution of 0.3 × 0.3 × 0.3 mm3, two averages, with a total scan time of 13:31 min per acquisition. This was acquired at five different scan sessions over a three‐month period and averaged together. After the final MRI session, the brain was perfusion‐fixed, extracted, and placed in 4% paraformaldehyde, then cryosectioned in the coronal plane at 20 μm thickness. To match the resolution of the highest‐resolution MRI scan, 1 in every 15 sections was retained, resulting in 300 μm spacing between sections. text: A T 2‐weighted MR image of a curved banana with an isotropic voxel resolution of 1 mm3 was obtained from The Possum Framework (Majka and Wojcik 2016). This image was reconstructed to provide a synthetic, structured test object for visualizing alignment accuracy and identifying spatial distortions. The Possum Framework provides both a reference shape and a corresponding distorted version of the banana dataset (https://github.com/pmajka/poSSum/tree/master). To generate a distorted banana dataset with known transformation files, we performed a slice‐wise 2D rigid and affine registration between the distorted (fixed) and reference (moving) volumes. The resulting transformations, capturing translations, rotations, scaling, and shearing, created synthetically distorted sections. These were restacked into a 3D moving volume for reconstruction.

text: To assess whether the proposed reconstruction framework generalizes to histological data that lacks a same‐specimen 3D reference volume, 10 parvalbumin‐stained histological sections from the Developmental Mouse Brain Atlas (DeMBA) (Bjerke et al. 2023) were reconstructed. A publicly available ex vivo T 2*‐weighted MRI dataset of a C57BL/6J mouse brain (Ma et al. 2005, 2008) was used as the anatomical reference volume. The MRI acquisition protocol is detailed in (Ma et al. 2005). Briefly, imaging was performed on a formalin‐fixed C57BL/6J mouse brain using a 3D gradient echo sequence on a 17.6T magnet with the following parameters: 47 μm resolution, TR = 150 ms, TE = 7.5 ms, flip angle = 25°. The histological and MRI datasets were obtained from the EBRAINS platform (https://search.kg.ebrains.eu/instances/0c2adfec‐6225‐400b‐b438‐c52ae7fbde2f) and NeuroImaging Tools & Resources Collaboratory (https://www.nitrc.org/projects/c57bl_mr_atlas/), respectively.

text: Tiles from all sections were first processed using BaSiC to estimate a specific flat‐field correction, which served as an initial baseline for subsequent section‐ and tile‐specific refinement. Full details of the tile‐level vignette correction are provided in Figure A1. Briefly, to improve local intensity consistency, overlapping regions between neighboring tiles were used to derive tile‐specific corrections. Processing was performed on a section‐by‐section basis, with the BaSiC flat‐field approximated by a fourth‐degree polynomial in both spatial dimensions for each tile. Pixel intensities within overlapping regions were then incorporated into a weighted least‐squares regression to refine the polynomial coefficients, enforcing agreement between overlapping tiles after correction. The BaSiC flat‐field estimate was weighted to 80% while the overlap consistency was weighted to 20%. To reduce computational burden, every 200th pixel was sampled for fitting, enabling execution on a desktop workstation with 64 GB of RAM. Algorithm performance was quantified using the Root Mean Squared Error (RMSE) computed between downsampled overlapping pixels in the log‐intensity domain across each section. text: Intensity normalization of the serial sections was performed prior to reconstruction to reduce section‐to‐section intensity variations. Each histological slice was first denoised using a 2D 8 × 8 pixel median filter. Tissue‐specific masks for gray matter (GM) and white matter (WM) were manually segmented in ITK‐SNAP (Yushkevich, Piven, et al. 2006) and used to compute the median intensity for each tissue class. Slice‐wise correction maps were calculated by dividing each pixel by its corresponding tissue median intensity. To prevent overcorrection near tissue boundaries, the tissue masks were dilated, and peripheral regions were assigned a neutral correction factor. A smooth 2D polynomial surface was subsequently fitted to each correction map to enforce spatial smoothness. The effectiveness of intensity normalization was quantified using the coefficient of variation (CV) of voxel intensities within tissue regions across all slices.

text: Prior to the image registration steps for the marmoset histological images, tile images in TIFF format (~1 GB each) underwent quality control. Quality control involved the removal of unusable slices and replacing them with neighboring sections when necessary. Full‐resolution images were downsampled by a factor of 100 and converted to PNG format to preserve the alpha channel. All image registrations were performed using Advanced Normalization Tools (ANTs) (Avants et al. 2008, 2011; Tustison et al. 2021). Landmark posts embedded in the blockface images facilitated registration. All posts were masked and aligned to a single masked reference post to ensure consistent imaging planes. After background removal, the transformation files from post‐registration were applied to the blockface images, converted to grayscale, and cropped to remove excess background.

text: The reconstruction pipeline follows the established Possum framework (Majka and Wojcik 2016; Yushkevich, Piven, et al. 2006; Yushkevich, Avants, et al. 2006) and consists of a multi‐stage registration strategy designed to balance global anatomical fidelity with local alignment accuracy. First, each histological slice is affinely registered to its corresponding reference slice (pairwise registration). Second, sequential registration to neighboring slices refines local alignment. Third, a coarse‐to‐fine step combines the high‐frequency components of the sequential transformations with the pairwise alignment, preserving global brain geometry while maintaining local edge structure. The marmoset T 1‐weighted anatomical MRI was first rigidly and then affinely registered in 3D to the blockface volume to align the reference anatomy with the blockface cutting plane (overview in Figure A2). Blockface reconstruction proceeded using the coarse‐to‐fine registration strategy. Nonlinear registration was intentionally omitted to avoid introducing geometric distortions inherent to MRI, thereby preserving the anatomical fidelity of the blockface volume to which the labeled section images will better align. The reconstructed blockface volume subsequently served as the reference space for histological reconstruction.

section: Integration of LSM Into the Possum Framework
text: The Possum Framework concludes with a deformable registration stage to correct residual local distortions. To improve robustness and anatomical plausibility during deformable registration, LSM‐based constraints were incorporated directly into the deformable registration. Key anatomical structures, such as the full tissue (GM + WM) and WM regions (Figure 1B), were manually segmented in ITK‐SNAP for both moving and fixed images. The resulting masks for each region of interest (Figure 1C,D) were used to compute level‐set maps (Figure 1E,F) using SimpleITK (Lowekamp et al. 2013). In these maps, the surface boundary is defined by the zero‐level set, interior values are negative, and exterior values are positive. These distance‐based representations encode both surface geometry and spatial context. The deformable registration step used a composite similarity metric combining mutual information (MI) between the moving and fixed image intensities and cross‐correlation (CC) between the corresponding level‐set representations. In contrast, the standard Possum framework relies solely on MI between fixed and moving image intensities. The inclusion of level‐set constraints provides explicit anatomical guidance, reducing instability in regions with weak tissue contrast. The synthetic banana MRI, histological

section: Improved Tile Stitching and Vignette Correction Through Overlap‐Aware Methods
text: Overlap‐aware correction significantly reduced residual shading and tile gridding across histological sections. A Friedman test on RMSE in overlapping regions (112 sections each with four fluorescent labels provides 448 measurements) revealed a significant effect of correction method (χ 2(2) = 890.04, p < 2.2e‐16), with post hoc Wilcoxon tests showing differences between all pairs (p < 2.2e‐16). These improvements are illustrated in Figure 2, which highlights cases with few, intermediate, and many tiles. BaSiC substantially improved shading in the raw data across all sections, while the overlap‐aware correction further reduced residual tile gridding under sparse coverage. When few tiles were available, the overlap‐aware method mitigated apparent gridding artifacts, though some residual effects remained due to its weighting toward the BaSiC solution (Figure 2A). With an intermediate number of tiles, the overlap‐aware correction successfully removed tile gridding in cases where BaSiC alone was insufficient (Figure 2B). For larger image sections containing many overlapping tiles, the overlap‐aware method performed comparably to BaSiC, effectively correcting shading artifacts within imaging tiles (Figure 2C).

section: Enhanced Alignment of Histology to Blockface Using LSM‐Constrained Registration
text: Incorporating LSM constraints into the deformable registration stage improved alignment of histological sections to blockface images. Qualitative assessment revealed that, relative to the coarse‐to‐fine baseline, the LSM‐integrated framework reduced local misalignment and better preserved the anatomical boundaries of GM and WM. Quantitatively, 2D/3D NMI increased from 0.4470/0.3929 to 0.4946/0.4301, and SSIM increased from 0.8022/0.7220 to 0.8297/0.7582, corresponding to improvements of approximately 10% in NMI and 3%–5% in SSIM. In contrast, the deformable method without LSM achieved more modest gains (NMI: ~3%; SSIM: ~0%–2%). These effects are illustrated in Figures 4 and 5 and summarized in Table 1. text: Incorporating LSM into the deformable registration stage improved anatomical continuity and structural fidelity in the reconstructed banana MRI volume. Compared with the standard Possum framework (without LSM), the LSM‐integrated approach reduced local misalignment and better preserved the internal structure of the synthetic object. These improvements are illustrated in Figure 7. Quantitative evaluation is summarized in Table A1. The LSM‐integrated framework achieved an RMSE of 1.676%, compared with 1.971% without LSM. Relative to the coarse‐to‐fine reconstruction baseline (2.286%), this corresponds to a 26.7% improvement. When compared directly with the deformable without LSM, the LSM‐integrated method shows a 15.0% improvement in RMSE. These improvements are further validated through absolute error maps (Figure 7H) between deformable with LSM (Figure 7F) and deformable without LSM (Figure 7G). These maps demonstrate reduced intensity differences when LSM constraints are applied, particularly in regions of high curvature.

section: LSM‐Integrated Framework Enhances Cross‐Specimen 3D Histological Reconstruction
text: Using unmatched MRI and histology from different mouse brains, the incorporation of LSM into the deformable registration stage substantially improved cross‐specimen 3D histological alignment, stabilizing the deformation and improving correspondence of pial boundaries and WM regions. Relative to the coarse‐to‐fine baseline, the LSM‐integrated framework increased 2D/3D NMI from 0.3010/0.2821 to 0.3462/0.3238 and SSIM from 0.4993/0.4914 to 0.5105/0.5007, corresponding to gains of ~14% in NMI and ~2% in SSIM. In comparison, the deformable method without level‐sets produced more modest improvements (NMI: 0.3042/0.2852; SSIM: 0.4999/0.4923). These effects are illustrated in Figure 8 and summarized in Table A2, highlighting the robust enhancement in volumetric and structural alignment achieved with LSM guidance.

text: In this work, we presented an integrated workflow combining vignette tile correction, slice normalization, and level‐set–guided deformable registration to improve the 3D reconstruction of serial histological sections. Together, these components address common sources of error in histological reconstruction, including spatial intensity inhomogeneity within tiles, variability between sections, and instability in deformable registration. Across multiple validation experiments, including synthetic datasets, blockface registration, and cross‐specimen reconstruction, the proposed framework improved anatomical continuity and structural correspondence, yielding consistent gains in RMSE, NMI, and SSIM. Microscopy data frequently exhibit spatial intensity inhomogeneities that can introduce stitching artifacts, intensity discontinuities, and errors in downstream analysis (Leong et al. 2003). Existing approaches, including low‐rank shading models and methods such as BaSiC (Peng et al. 2017), provide effective correction when sufficient tile overlap is available but may be limited under sparse tile coverage or when tile‐specific corrections are required (Smith et al. 2015). Our results demonstrate that overlap‐aware vignette correction effectively reduces residual gridding artifacts across varying tile counts. When many tiles were present, the method performed comparably to BaSiC, while under sparse coverage, it provided improved
title: Improved Post-Processing Framework for Whole Slide Imaging and 3D Reconstruction

text: overlap‐aware vignette correction effectively reduces residual gridding artifacts across varying tile counts. When many tiles were present, the method performed comparably to BaSiC, while under sparse coverage, it provided improved correction by explicitly leveraging overlap information between neighboring tiles. These findings suggest that incorporating overlap information provides a robust and adaptable approach for shading correction in whole‐slide imaging, improving both shading uniformity and tile alignment across diverse acquisition settings. Inter‐section intensity variability is another major challenge in serial histology reconstruction. Differences in section thickness, stain penetration, fixation quality, and slide preparation can produce large variations in overall intensity between slices (Al‐Kinani 2024). Without appropriate normalization, these variations can bias similarity metrics used during registration, causing algorithms to interpret intensity differences as structural discrepancies and ultimately degrading alignment accuracy (Maes et al. 1997). Conventional global normalization approaches standardize overall intensity distributions but may compress biologically meaningful contrast between tissue compartments. In contrast, the proposed approach normalizes GM and WM independently using their respective median intensities, preserving intrinsic tissue contrast while reducing inter‐section variability. Modeling the correction factor with a low‐order polynomial

text: contrast, the proposed approach normalizes GM and WM independently using their respective median intensities, preserving intrinsic tissue contrast while reducing inter‐section variability. Modeling the correction factor with a low‐order polynomial further enforces spatial smoothness, allowing macroscopic intensity variation to be corrected while maintaining fine anatomical detail. To address geometric distortions that arise during sectioning and mounting, we introduced a deformable registration framework incorporating LSM as structural constraints. Across all datasets, integrating LSM into the deformable stage consistently improved performance relative to both the coarse‐to‐fine baseline and deformable approaches without LSM guidance. In the marmoset histology‐to‐blockface experiment, LSM integration increased both 2D and 3D similarity metrics and visually stabilized deformations in regions prone to local misalignment. In the synthetic banana dataset, inclusion of LSM reduced RMSE, indicating improved structural continuity and reduced local misalignment. Similarly, in the mouse histology reconstruction, LSM‐guided registration improved NMI and SSIM, reflecting better correspondence of pial and WM boundaries. These results suggest that augmenting deformable registration with structural constraints derived from level sets provides a consistent and meaningful improvement in alignment accuracy. These results suggest that augmenting deformable registration with structural constraints derived from level sets provides a consistent and meaningful improvement in alignment accuracy. An advantage of this framework is its flexibility in incorporating reference information. While optimal results are expected when the reference image originates from the same specimen, such as blockface imaging or MRI, the method can also operate using references from different subjects or modalities, including computed tomography (CT). In this study, level‐set maps were generated from manually segmented masks, but this step could also be implemented using automated segmentation tools or existing anatomical atlases. Consequently, the approach is not limited to histological brain reconstruction but may apply to other serial imaging datasets where distortions must be corrected. Three‐dimensional reconstruction from serial histological sections is an increasingly active area of research, with large‐scale initiatives such as BigBrain (Amunts et al. 2013) and BigMac (Howard et al. 2022), and maps of cyto‐ and fiber architecture of the human brain (Alkemade et al. 2022). This work also spans region‐specific reconstructions of structures including the hippocampus (Adler et
title: Improved Post-Processing Framework for Whole Slide Imaging and 3D Reconstruction

text: al. 2022), and maps of cyto‐ and fiber architecture of the human brain (Alkemade et al. 2022). This work also spans region‐specific reconstructions of structures including the hippocampus (Adler et al. 2014), basal ganglia and thalamus (Chakravarty et al. 2006), and non‐human primate brains such as the owl monkey (Choe et al. 2011) and baboon (Dauguet et al. 2007). Other studies have applied similar reconstruction approaches to non‐neural tissues, including prostate (Gibson et al. 2013) and liver (Song et al. 2013). While these efforts demonstrate the feasibility of high‐resolution 3D reconstruction, many rely on dataset‐specific processing pipelines, extensive manual intervention, or carefully controlled acquisition protocols. As a result, generalizability across tissues, staining protocols, and experimental conditions remains a persistent challenge. By incorporating level‐set constraints within the deformable stage, the framework presented here provides a structurally guided mechanism to stabilize reconstruction without relying on extensive manual landmark placement or dataset‐specific parameter tuning. Importantly, the ability to incorporate level‐set information within defined regions of interest allows the method to extend beyond whole‐brain reconstruction to organ‐specific applications.

text: Several limitations of the proposed framework warrant consideration. The overlap‐aware intensity correction relies on the presence of sufficient and accurately registered overlap regions between tiles. When overlap is minimal, tiling geometry is irregular, or tile positions are inaccurately estimated, the correction may become under‐constrained or propagate boundary inconsistencies across tiles. In addition, the method assumes that illumination inhomogeneity varies smoothly across the field of view. While appropriate for vignetting and large‐scale shading effects, this assumption may limit the correction of abrupt illumination changes or tile‐specific acquisition artifacts. The tissue‐class‐specific intensity normalization reduces inter‐slice variability but currently relies on manually generated segmentations, introducing additional labor and potential observer‐dependent variability. Although automated segmentation methods could mitigate this limitation, they were not evaluated in this study. Furthermore, the normalization assumes relatively consistent intra‐class intensity distributions across sections. While this stabilizes similarity metrics and improves alignment robustness, it may attenuate subtle biologically meaningful contrast variations in regions with heterogeneous staining or pathology. Finally, although LSM provides a strong structural constraint during deformable registration, it cannot fully compensate for distortions inherent to histological processing. When

Finally, although LSM provides a strong structural constraint during deformable registration, it cannot fully compensate for distortions inherent to histological processing. When external reference atlases are used, anatomical differences between specimens may introduce bias, particularly in regions with substantial inter‐subject variability. Optimal performance is therefore expected when specimen‐specific references, such as blockface imaging or same‐subject MRI, are available. Acquiring a post‐mortem MRI prior to tissue processing may further reduce registration bias by providing a subject‐specific reference that captures fixation‐ and shrinkage‐related distortions before histological sectioning. Additionally, deformable registration cannot reconstruct missing tissue or fully correct severe artifacts such as tears, folds, or compression introduced during sectioning. In this study, we presented an integrated framework for 3D histological reconstruction that combines overlap‐aware tile correction, tissue‐specific intensity normalization, and LSM‐guided deformable registration. Across synthetic, single‐subject, and cross‐specimen datasets, the proposed workflow improved structural fidelity, volumetric alignment, and inter‐slice intensity consistency relative to conventional approaches. By providing a robust and flexible reconstruction pipeline, this framework enables reproducible 3D reconstruction of serial histological data and supports

text: With the increasing adoption of 3D cell cultures and bioprinting in biomedical research, there is a growing demand for reliable and accurate monitoring methods. While fluorescence microscopy is widely accepted for 2D cell cultures, when introducing the third dimension it often suffers from signal attenuation and out‐of‐focus interference, making automated image analysis challenging. In this study, a hybrid pipeline that integrates deep learning and traditional image processing techniques is presented with the aim of establishing an automated tool for cell segmentation and viability assessment in 3D from fluorescence microscopy images. A U 2‐Net architecture was trained on 2D cell cultures for cell segmentation, while watershed‐based separation and intensity‐based classification were employed for viability detection. The model demonstrated accurate segmentation with minimal overfitting. Quantitative comparisons with manual counts and ImageJ‐based results confirmed its accuracy. We then demonstrated the possibility of extending this model to 3D constructs by tracking cell density and viability during time in the case of human umbilical vein endothelial cells bioprinted in gelatin methacrylate at different seeding densities, taken as case study. Automated counts closely matched manual ones,

text: In recent years, three‐dimensional (3D) cell cultures and bioprinted constructs have emerged as a promising technology in biomedical research due to their ability to better replicate the physiological and structural complexity of native tissues compared to traditional two‐dimensional (2D) monolayers (Sharma et al. 2023; Breslin and O’Driscoll 2013). In particular, bioprinting can be defined as the layer‐by‐layer deposition of biocompatible materials, mostly biopolymers, containing living cells and other biological factors on the basis of a computer‐aided design. This technology finds application in a variety of areas, ranging from tissue engineering to regenerative medicine, clinics, drug screening, and disease modeling (Ozbolat 2015; Ozbolat et al. 2016). Among a variety of 3D bioprinting strategies, extrusion‐based bioprinting is the most widely used due to its ability to deposit cells and biomaterials with high spatial precision and reduced mechanical and chemical stresses, facilitating the fabrication of complex, multicellular constructs (Salaris and Rosa 2019; Heinrich et al. 2019; Matai et al. 2019). With the growing diffusion of 3D constructs, there is a corresponding need for reliable methods to assess cell behavior within these environments and

text: et al. 2019; Matai et al. 2019). With the growing diffusion of 3D constructs, there is a corresponding need for reliable methods to assess cell behavior within these environments and track their viability and density over time. Fluorescence microscopy, particularly live/dead assays using dual fluorescent staining, remains the standard technique adopted for assessing cell viability. In fact, it offers good accuracy while being a nondestructive technique, hence suitable for in situ monitoring. However, the transition from 2D to 3D imaging presents new challenges. Image quality deteriorates in 3D samples due to reduced optical transparency, signal attenuation with depth, and increased out‐of‐focus interference, thus complicating quantitative analysis (Smith et al. 2010; Bikmulina et al. 2022). A recent work reported the in situ analysis of cell spatial distribution during the bioprinting of 3D constructs by fluorescence imaging, providing a promising solution to overcome the mentioned challenges, while at the same time automatizing the process (Margarita et al. 2025). However, the accurate quantification of live and dead cells from fluorescence images remains a critical and often limiting step in experimental workflows (Piccinini et

text: the process (Margarita et al. 2025). However, the accurate quantification of live and dead cells from fluorescence images remains a critical and often limiting step in experimental workflows (Piccinini et al. 2014; O'Brien et al. 2016; He et al. 2019). Manual counting is still commonly employed but it is time‐consuming, subjective, and not scalable for high‐throughput experiments. Semi‐automated methods exist, but they often rely on expensive instrumentation or require well‐separated cells and uniform signal intensity to be effective (Lavitt et al. 2021; De Boodt et al. 2013). Reliable cell quantification first requires accurate segmentation, differentiating cells from the background, which is highly sensitive to image features like brightness, contrast, and signal uniformity. This task becomes especially challenging in dense or noisy samples, where cells overlap or exhibit weak fluorescence signals. Although open‐source tools, such as ImageJ and CellProfiler, offer modular pipelines, frequently addressing specific segmentation problems, they require the combination of multiple techniques and a manual fine‐tuning of the corresponding parameters. Given the rigidity of the architecture, even small variations in image quality, such as changes in illumination, background noise,

Given the rigidity of the architecture, even small variations in image quality, such as changes in illumination, background noise, or staining intensity, can significantly degrade segmentation performance, often necessitating repeated and labor‐intensive adjustments (Wang et al. 2018). As a result, existing workflows tend to suffer from poor reproducibility, low transferability, and over‐ or underestimation under challenging conditions (De Boodt et al. 2013; Wang et al. 2018). Recent advances in machine learning, particularly deep learning, have significantly improved the automation and accuracy of image analysis tasks. Among CNN architectures, U 2‐Net has demonstrated strong performance in image segmentation tasks, being more and more considered for applications in biomedical image analysis (Wang et al. 2018; Yamashita et al. 2018; Li et al. 2024; Antonelli et al. 2022; Azad et al. 2024; Tan et al. 2026; Huo et al. 2025; Fang et al. 2024). This network has gained attention for its effectiveness in salient object detection (SOB) through a nested U‐structure that allows for high resolution while maintaining computational efficiency (Qin et al. 2020). However, deep learning models still face some difficulties when dealing with densely packed or connected cells, as accurately detecting thin boundaries is challenging with limited labeled data. The lack of standardized, diverse training datasets for different cell types and imaging conditions further limits the performance of these models. text: datasets for different cell types and imaging conditions further limits the performance of these models. Recent studies have been proposed to overcome the issue of limited annotated datasets (Zhou et al. 2024; Zargari et al. 2024). A relevant example is the work from Çelebi et al., who demonstrated that representation‐level self‐supervised contrastive learning improved Mask R‐CNN‐based senescent cell segmentation in brightfield microscopy images, increasing downstream segmentation performance compared with the original segmentation model (Çelebi et al. 2024). However, common imaging artifacts, such as blurring, noise, and focus drift, can compromise segmentation quality, emphasizing the need for robust, adaptable solutions that perform reliably in experimental setups (Wang et al. 2018). To address these challenges, this work proposes a fully automated pipeline for cell segmentation and viability assessment from fluorescence microscopy images in the specific case of human umbilical vein endothelial cells (HUVECs), chosen as a model system. The methodology consists of a two‐stage pipeline: (1) U 2‐Net‐based segmentation for accurate cell boundary detection, and (2) watershed‐based separation and intensity‐based classification for quantifying live and total cells. By integrating both deep learning

text: a two‐stage pipeline: (1) U 2‐Net‐based segmentation for accurate cell boundary detection, and (2) watershed‐based separation and intensity‐based classification for quantifying live and total cells. By integrating both deep learning and traditional algorithms, this hybrid approach mitigates the limitations of each of them: it achieves high segmentation accuracy while remaining adaptable to different imaging conditions without requiring extensive manual tuning or retraining. The pipeline developed in this work is schematized in Figure 1. We initially developed this tool from 2D HUVEC cultures, enabling facile handling and the acquisition of a robust dataset from brightfield and fluorescence microscopy images. In fact, the cells were transfected to express the green fluorescent protein (GFP) as free cytoplasmatic protein, which was taken as indicator of viable cells. In addition, before seeding, HUVECs were stained with Rhodamine B‐tagged polymer nanoparticles to provide a red fluorescence signal, taken to estimate the total cells (i.e., dead + live). These images were used for hyperparameter selection and model training. text: live). These images were used for hyperparameter selection and model training. The comparison of the results from a validation dataset, excluded from the calibration stage, with manually counted cells confirmed the accuracy of the model in both segmentation and viability classification. We then demonstrated its translatability to 3D bioprinted constructs, where this model allowed the accurate tracking of cell density and viability for HUVECs in gelatin methacrylate structures in a fully automated way. Moreover, this protocol avoided the need for sacrificing the constructs, as it is required with traditional live/dead assays. Overall, the pipeline modular implementation allows for easy integration into a wide range of microscopy workflows. This of course may require dedicated model training based on the specific system used but the advantage would then be a significant reduction in user workload, enhancement of reproducibility, and high‐throughput fluorescence image analysis.

text: HUVECs transiently transfected with the turbo green fluorescent protein (turboGFP) vector were acquired from Innoprot (Spain), catalog number P20201, and used as a cell model. Cells were cultured in endothelial cell growth medium (PromoCell, Germany), supplemented with 1% w/v penicillin/streptomycin (Sigma‐Aldrich, St. Louis, USA) at 37°C, 5% v/v CO2, 95% humidity in a Forma Steri‐Cycle CO2 Incubator. Cells were used between passages 6 and 8. To enable dual fluorescence imaging, cells were treated with rhodamine B‐labeled polymethyl methacrylate nanoparticles at a concentration of 0.3 mg/mL, 24 h before imaging. The nanoparticles were synthesized as reported by Dossi et al. (2013). While GFP provided a green fluorescence signal for viable cells, the rhodamine‐labeled nanoparticles allowed the detection of the total cells (viable + dead).

This ink was then crosslinked under UV light (365 nm, 60 s) to form a thin hydrogel layer at the bottom of each well of a 48‐well plate. HUVECs were then seeded at a density of 30,000 cells/cm2 on top of the GelMA layer and routinely grown in endothelial cell growth medium as reported in Section 2.1.1. After counting, the suspension was adjusted to the desired cell concentration, i.e., 50 × 106 cells/mL. text: Images were acquired using the Celena S digital microscope (Logos Biosystems, South Korea). For each sample, images were acquired in triplicate in three channels: brightfield, green, and red fluorescence. For green fluorescence signal, a LED filter cube with excitation wavelength 470 nm and bandwidth 30 nm and emission wavelength 530 nm and bandwidth 50 nm was used. For the red fluorescence signal, the installed filter allowed excitation at 530 nm with bandwidth 40 nm and emission at 605 nm with bandwidth 55 nm. Acquisitions were performed at magnifications 10× and 20× with a resolution of 1280 × 1024 pixels. Brightness and contrast settings were manually adjusted before imaging. The exposure time was automatically adjusted for each acquisition from the imaging software of the microscope. Once established, the same microscope settings were maintained for all acquisitions to ensure consistency among images. The same acquisition settings were maintained during image collection, and the fluorescence intensity thresholds used for cell classification were applied uniformly to all images without image‐specific adjustments. All three channels were used for segmentation to exploit the information provided by

text: A total of 42 2D images were manually annotated for training and testing. These where then randomly subdivided in two datasets. Specifically, 36 images were used for training, while 6 were reserved for testing. The images were manually labeled by the author using ImageJ (FIJI) software, assisted by the magic wand tool to select individual cells, followed by manual refinement where necessary. Binary masks separating cells from the background were produced as ground truth references for training and testing.

text: Before training, images were enhanced using the rolling ball algorithm to improve contrast between background and cells, facilitating segmentation. Images were then divided into patches of size 512 × 512 pixels with a stride of 256 pixels. Several data augmentation techniques were applied to the images and their corresponding masks using the Albumentations library to improve the model robustness and generalization ability. These included random horizontal and vertical flipping, random rotations, and the ShiftScaleRotate transformation, which performs random shifts, zooming, and rotations. After this process, a total of 1296 images were obtained for training, and 216 for testing. Then, channel‐wise normalization was performed to standardize input data and facilitate model convergence during training. For each of the three input channels (brightfield, green fluorescence, and red fluorescence), grayscale images were converted to tensors, and the mean (μ) and standard deviation (σ) of pixel intensity values were computed across the training dataset. These values were then used to normalize each image according to Equation (1). (1) Normalized Pixel=Pixel Intensity−μσ

text: A patch size of 512 × 512 pixels with a stride of 256 pixels was adopted after testing multiple combinations (512 × 512, 320 × 320 pixels; stride of 512, 320, 256 pixels). The hyperparameters were selected based on a tradeoff between computational time and quality of the segmentation, quantified through the binary cross‐entropy (BCE) in validation as loss function. A training limit of 100 epochs was chosen to ensure sufficient time for convergence, while early stopping (patience = 5) was implemented to avoid overfitting and reduce training time. The initial learning rate was set to 1 × 10−5. Batch sizes of 4, 8, 16, and 32 were tested.

text: For the segmentation task, the U 2‐Net architecture was used. The model was initialized with random weights and trained from scratch using the three input channels along with their corresponding ground truth binary masks. The dataset was divided into two subsets: 80% of the images were used for training, and 20% were reserved for validation. The validation set was used to monitor performance during training and ensure the model generalized well to unseen data. The model was trained using the previously defined hyperparameters and the Adam optimizer, which is particularly suited for problems with sparse gradients and noisy data. BCE was used as the loss function, commonly applied for binary segmentation tasks. Training and validation losses were tracked at each epoch to monitor convergence and detect overfitting. Additionally, the Dice score was computed at the end of each epoch for both training and validation datasets as the overlap between ground truth labels and model results as in Equation (2) (Seghier 2024). (2) Dice score=2TP2TP+FP+FN where TP are the true positive results, which is the number of counts correctly predicted by
title: A Deep Learning Pipeline for Cell Segmentation and Viability Quantification in 3D Constructs From Fluorescence Microscopy Images

text: truth labels and model results as in Equation (2) (Seghier 2024). (2) Dice score=2TP2TP+FP+FN where TP are the true positive results, which is the number of counts correctly predicted by the model; FP are the false positives, i.e., cells wrongly identified by the model; FN are the false negatives, i.e., cells labeled manually and not recognized by the model. To ensure optimal performance, the final model used for evaluation was selected based on the epoch with the highest validation Dice score. After training, the model was tested on a separate test set comprising 216 image patches derived from six full‐resolution 2D images not used during training or validation. The Dice coefficient was computed for each batch in the test set.

text: After segmentation, the resulting binary masks underwent a post‐processing step to identify live and dead cells. First, masks were refined by excluding regions with fluorescence intensities (in both red and green channels) below a predefined threshold, with the aim of removing background noise and artifacts not related to cells. Next, a watershed algorithm was applied using the watershed function of the skimage library to separate touching or overlapping cells. Following segmentation, each labeled region in the binary mask was analyzed. A minimum area threshold of 50 pixels2 was set, as this value is below the expected area covered by a single cell at 10× magnification, thus allowing the removal of small artifacts. For the remaining regions, mean fluorescence intensities in the red and green channels were computed. Classification was then performed based on these intensity values: regions with both red and green signals were classified as live cells; regions with only red signal were classified as dead cells. Specifically, a segmented region was classified as a live cell when the mean green fluorescence intensity exceeded 8 (8‐bit grayscale). On the
title: A Deep Learning Pipeline for Cell Segmentation and Viability Quantification in 3D Constructs From Fluorescence Microscopy Images

text: only red signal were classified as dead cells. Specifically, a segmented region was classified as a live cell when the mean green fluorescence intensity exceeded 8 (8‐bit grayscale). On the other side, no threshold was set on the red channel, because the rhodamine fluorescence signal was consistently weaker than the green fluorescence one. The selected thresholds were applied consistently to all images without image‐specific adjustment.

text: To validate the model ability to generalize to unseen data and evaluate its performance in practical applications, a set of 70 images from 2D monolayer cultures was used. Each image was manually counted three times, and the average of these counts was used as a reference value for comparison with the model counts. This approach aimed to minimize human error and provide a more consistent ground truth for evaluating model accuracy. Performance was assessed by calculating different statistical metrics commonly used for regression tasks. In particular, the Mean Absolute Error (MAE), Root Mean Square Error (RMSE), Coefficient of Determination (R 2), and the Pearson correlation coefficient (r) were adopted for live and total cells. For 3D experiments, quantitative validation against manual annotations was not feasible due to the intrinsic complexity of manually segmenting and counting cells within volumetric constructs. Instead, the evaluation focused on qualitative and application‐oriented validation. Model outputs were visually inspected across multiple regions of interest to qualitatively assess segmentation accuracy and robustness. Furthermore, model counts in GelMA‐based constructs were compared with manual annotations in a case study

text: The pipeline was implemented in Python 3.12.4. The core libraries used in this work included PyTorch (version 2.6.0) for model definition and training, Torchvision (version 0.21.0) for dataset handling and transformations, and Albumentations (version 2.0.4) for data augmentation. Image processing relied on OpenCV (version 4.11.0.86), Scikit‐image (version 0.25.2), SciPy (version 1.15.1), and PIL (version 11.1.0). Data analysis and visualization were performed using NumPy (version 2.2.2), Pandas (version 2.2.3), Seaborn (version 0.13.2), and Matplotlib (version 3.10.0). The U 2‐Net architecture was imported from a local implementation of the original model repository (source: https://github.com/xuebinqin/u‐2‐net). All training and inference operations were run on a CPU system with 64.0 GB of RAM. No GPU was used.

text: In this work, green fluorescent HUVECs were selected for model development and testing. These were incubated with rhodamine B‐labeled polymethyl methacrylate nanoparticles for a red staining before seeding. This strategy provided dual fluorescence microscopy trackability: the green channel could in fact be exploited to detect viable cells, while the red channel was considered representative of both live and dead cells. Images of the cell cultures were acquired at 10× and 20× magnifications for both 2D monolayer cultures and 3D bioprinted constructs across three channels: brightfield, green fluorescence (GFP), and red fluorescence (rhodamine‐labeled nanoparticles). For 3D constructs, images were captured at different focal planes along the z‐axis to account for the sample thickness. Out‐of‐focus signals from cells outside the selected focal plane were excluded during post‐processing through threshold‐based filtering, ensuring that only well‐focused cells were considered for subsequent analysis. text: To identify the most effective patching strategy, different combinations of patch size and stride were tested. As shown in Table 1, the configuration using 512 × 512 pixel patches with a 256‐pixel stride yielded the highest Dice score (0.7403), outperforming both smaller patches and configurations with larger strides. The hyperparameter values were selected through iterative testing, aiming to balance segmentation accuracy, training efficiency, and hardware limitations. All experiments were performed on a CPU‐based workstation without GPU acceleration. Table 2 reports the results of this analysis performed at fixed learning rate of 1 × 10 −5 and at different batch size. The loss initially decreased with the batch size, indicating a progressive increase in the segmentation performance. However, this is accompanied by a decisive increase in the time required for model training. Among the tested values, a batch size of 16 provided the best compromise between computational time and performance and was therefore selected for the following tasks.

text: By selecting these parameters, the training and validation loss and Dice score over 70 epochs are shown in Figure 4a,b. Although the training limit was set to 100 epochs, early stopping (patience = 5) was applied to prevent overfitting and reduce unnecessary computation, which resulted in training stopping at epoch 70. The loss curves indicate consistent convergence, with both training and validation loss decreasing steadily. However, the validation loss reaches a plateau earlier, suggesting potential overfitting after approximately 30 epochs. The segmentation performance improves rapidly during the initial epochs, as confirmed by the steep decrease in the loss function and increase in the Dice score. However, while the Dice score for the training steadily increases, the same metric referred to the validation dataset reaches a plateau and shows minor fluctuations after epoch 20. The observed gap between training and validation Dice scores reflects a modest overfitting trend. To address this, the final model used for evaluation was selected based on the highest validation Dice score, corresponding to epoch 65, where it reached a value of 0.8433, indicating effective segmentation performance.

text: After having developed the algorithm able to differentiate and automatically count live and dead cells, the model performance was quantitatively validated on a manually annotated set of 70 2D images. Manual counts were performed three times per image, and the mean count was used as the reference. This approach aimed to reduce variability due to subjectivity and human error and ensure more reliable annotations. While 3D samples were also segmented and analyzed by the model, manual annotation of 3D data was not considered for model validation due to the complexity and subjectivity of manual cell counting in 3D images. On the other side, the model results on 3D samples were compared to manual counts for a specific case study of bioprinted cells in the following Section. The model reliability was evaluated considering four metrics: MAE, RMSE, determination coefficient (R 2), and Pearson correlation coefficient (r), focusing on live and total cell counts, which are the direct outputs from the model, assessed by evaluating green and red labeled cells, respectively. Metrics for dead cells and vitality were not evaluated separately, as

The number of total cells and live cells was then tracked over time by acquiring and analyzing images at three time points: Day 1, 3, and 7. Even if some variability is present in the absolute cell numbers, likely due to the inherent subjectivity and limitations of manual annotation, the values obtained from the model closely follow the same trend as the manual counts across all time points and conditions. Importantly, the segmentation remains accurate even for cells that are barely distinguishable by eye, demonstrating the sensitivity, and reliability of the model. text: for cells that are barely distinguishable by eye, demonstrating the sensitivity, and reliability of the model. To quantitatively evaluate the agreement between the two counting methodologies, a paired analysis was conducted across all 27 experimental observations (three replicates for each condition). The automated model showed a strong correlation with manual counts, yielding Pearson correlation coefficients of r=0.9631 (p<0.001) for live cells and r=0.9665 (p<0.001) for total cells, with corresponding R2 of 0.8714 and 0.8684, respectively. The accuracy of the automated counts was further supported by low MAE and RMSE values, equal to 4.85 and 6.96 cells/image for live counts and 5.22 and 7.10 cells/image for total counts, respectively. A minor systematic underestimation was observed (mean bias of −3.22 cells/image for live cells and −4.19 cells/image for total cells), which may be partly attributable to overlapping cells in complex 3D regions. This example demonstrates the practical utility of the developed model for real‐world applications. By automating the cell viability assessment, the model significantly reduces the time and effort required for manual quantification, offering a valid alternative for routine biological experiments.

text: With the increasing attention to 3D bioprinting in biomedical research, the need for reliable methods to assess cell viability in complex 3D constructs has become increasingly important. Automated analysis in such structures is challenging due to signal attenuation, optical transparency, and out‐of‐focus interference. This study presents a hybrid, fully automated pipeline that integrates deep learning and traditional image processing to enable accurate segmentation and viability assessment in fluorescence microscopy images. The proposed approach offers a valid alternative to manual or semi‐automated workflows, reducing manual workload. For segmentation, the U 2‐Net architecture was trained from scratch, with hyperparameters such as batch size, learning rate, and patch size optimized through iterative testing to find a balance between segmentation accuracy and computational efficiency. The final configuration, using a patch size of 512 × 512 pixels with a stride of 256 pixels, demonstrated strong performance, with a validation Dice score of 0.8433. The training process showed consistent convergence and minimal overfitting, as indicated by both Dice score and BCE loss. Model performance was quantitatively evaluated by comparing both manual and ImageJ‐based counts through the
title: A Deep Learning Pipeline for Cell Segmentation and Viability Quantification in 3D Constructs From Fluorescence Microscopy Images

text: process showed consistent convergence and minimal overfitting, as indicated by both Dice score and BCE loss. Model performance was quantitatively evaluated by comparing both manual and ImageJ‐based counts through the evaluation of multiple metrics (MAE, RMSE, R 2, and Pearson's correlation coefficient). The results of this analysis indicated improved accuracy in predicting the number of cells, particularly for total cell counts. To showcase the model applicability in a real experiment, the cell density was tracked during time in GelMA‐based 3D constructs. Automated cell counts were compared with manual annotations. While minor discrepancies in absolute cell numbers were observed, likely due to variability in manual counting, the model accurately captured temporal trends in cell proliferation. In summary, the proposed pipeline is a reliable and efficient tool for cell segmentation and viability analysis from fluorescence microscopy images. It offers a solution for high‐throughput workflows, particularly where manual annotation is infeasible or error‐prone.

text: New in vitro models are urgently needed to improve the preclinical development of new drugs. Current standardised cellular models are mainly based on 2D cell culture, which lacks physiological flow conditions and often involves limited or simplified co-culture settings. • Organ-on-a-chip (OoC) systems use microchips incorporating extracellular matrices, surface coatings and cell cultures to mimic physiological conditions, enabling the formation of 3D structures, co-culture systems and dynamic flow. However, to perform reproducible and controlled experiments using OoC systems, it is necessary to systematically standardise cell culture conditions within the microfluidic channels. • The selection of the extracellular matrix (ECM) coating of the chip must be tailored and optimised for each specific cell type used in OoC systems. It is essential to establish the appropriate biological microenvironment following cell adhesion to the chip, including the time required for cell adhesion and maturation, as well as the appropriate flow conditions. • This protocol standardises flow and ECM coating conditions in OoC with kidney (Caki-1) and lung (A549) cell lines, facilitating reproducible experiments and enabling broader application across different OoC models.

text: New in vitro models are urgently needed to improve both the quality of research data and the preclinical development of new drugs. Multiwell 2D cell culture models have been widely used for almost 100 years [1], however, these culture conditions are not optimal for obtaining reliable and physiologically relevant biological data. More recently, alternatives to these traditional culture systems have been developed, including advanced 3D cellular models such as organoids, spheroids and organ-on-a-chip (OoC) systems. Among these models, OoC technology has emerged as a revolutionary approach in biomedical research. These sophisticated 3D models mimic physiological tissular architecture and enable the generation of customised cellular microenvironments with precise fluidic and structural control [[2], [3], [4]]. These models have emerged as an improvement over both conventional 2D cell culture [5] and animal models, which, although widely used, often generate results that cannot be directly translated to humans [[6], [7], [8]]. Compared with conventional 2D cell models, OoC systems exhibit differences in biological behaviour, including cellular migration and proliferation [9,10], cell-cycle regulation and metabolic pathways [10] and, importantly, a more physiologically relevant response
title: Systematic standardization of organ-on-a-chip under controlled flow conditions: Use case with Caki-1 and A549 cell lines

text: conventional 2D cell models, OoC systems exhibit differences in biological behaviour, including cellular migration and proliferation [9,10], cell-cycle regulation and metabolic pathways [10] and, importantly, a more physiologically relevant response to treatments [11,12]. Importantly, the characteristics and underlying concept of OoC technology may contribute to reducing and partially replacing the use of animals in research. In particular, these models may help address interspecies differences and ethical concerns associated with animal experimentation [13]. The combination of the advantages of in vitro models with increased physiological complexity [14] has generated considerable interest in the application of OoC systems as preclinical in vitro models. These systems provide a highly controlled cellular environment, good reproducibility and relatively straightforward assembly. Flow within the chip is a relevant factor because it reproduces wall shear stress conditions [15], which can elicit biological responses affecting cell differentiation, morphology and metabolism [16], thereby providing a closer representation of the physiological environment [17]. The type and the pattern of flow depend on both the geometry of the chip and the external perfusion system, resulting in different flow profiles and, consequently,
title: Systematic standardization of organ-on-a-chip under controlled flow conditions: Use case with Caki-1 and A549 cell lines

text: physiological environment [17]. The type and the pattern of flow depend on both the geometry of the chip and the external perfusion system, resulting in different flow profiles and, consequently, distinct cellular responses [18]. Another relevant factor mimicking the physiological microenvironment and enabling cells to withstand flow is the nature of the cell-adhesion surface. Polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS) is a widely used material for OoC fabrication owing to its attractive properties, including biocompatibility, gas permeability and favourable mechanical and optical properties [19]. However, PDMS is inherently hydrophobic, which results in poor cell-adhesion capacity. Consequently, biological functionalisation plays a central role in OoC development, with extracellular matrix (ECM) coatings being one of the most widely used strategies to improve surface hydrophilicity [20] and provide chemical (such as hydroxyl, amine or carboxyl groups) and biological cues (such as peptide sequences) that promote cell attachment. Different ECM coatings can influence cellular responses [21], resulting in differences in cell adhesion, biomarker production, growth rate, morphology and tight-junction protein expression [22,23]. As OoC systems offer promising applications in drug research, particularly for evaluating the efficacy and toxicity
title: Systematic standardization of organ-on-a-chip under controlled flow conditions: Use case with Caki-1 and A549 cell lines

text: differences in cell adhesion, biomarker production, growth rate, morphology and tight-junction protein expression [22,23]. As OoC systems offer promising applications in drug research, particularly for evaluating the efficacy and toxicity of compounds, the development of reliable and accurate in vitro models is essential. Characterisation of both flow conditions and optimised ECM coatings in newly developed OoC systems will enable the generation of high-quality, reproducible models of human organs and diseases. In this work, we experimentally standardised flow parameters and ECM coating conditions using two cell lines derived from lung (A549) and kidney (Caki-1) tissues. This approach enabled us to establish optimised conditions to ensure the reliability and consistency of OoC models.

The ability of cells cultured in an OoC system to withstand flow is directly related to the quality of cell adhesion and the establishment of an appropriate biological microenvironment. Therefore, it is important to determine the critical flow levels that these cell lines can withstand in order to establish the upper limit of wall shear stress suitable for OoC experiments. Wall shear stress was calculated using the Hagen–Poiseuille equation for a circular channel, τ = 4μQ/πR³, where µ is dynamic viscosity, Q is the volumetric flow rate and π is the constant. text: In summary, three main considerations should be addressed when implementing experimental procedures in OoC systems under flow conditions. First, the selection of the ECM or surface coating of the chip must be tailored and optimised for each specific cell type. Different cell types exhibit varying adhesion capacities, and not all materials or surface coatings are suitable for cell culture. As cells in these systems are exposed to wall shear stress generated by fluid flow, it is crucial to ensure robust cell adhesion and its maintenance throughout the experiment. As demonstrated in this study, the incorporation of fibronectin into the surface coating enhanced cell adhesion in both the Caki-1 and A549 cell lines. Second, it is essential to establish an appropriate biological microenvironment following cell adhesion to the chip. This can be achieved by optimising several parameters, including allowing sufficient time for cell adaptation and maturation within the chip, using an appropriate culture medium, and applying a low flow rate before exposing the cells to the final experimental conditions. These steps are essential to ensure optimal cellular performance during subsequent experimental

These steps are essential to ensure optimal cellular performance during subsequent experimental procedures. Finally, the aim of OoC experiments is to analyse cellular behaviour and responses within a novel microenvironment under flow conditions. This requires the measurement and consideration of additional parameters to accurately assess cell functionality. Furthermore, it is important to recognise that these experiments may provide new insights into cellular responses that have previously been characterised under static culture conditions.

text: Environmental pollutants pose an escalating health threat, yet traditional toxicity models are inherently limited in recapitulating complex human physiology. As an emerging organ-on-a-chip technology, microfluidic lung-on-a-chip employs microengineering approaches to precisely replicate the key structural features and dynamic physiological microenvironment of the human lung in vitro, thereby providing a highly biomimetic research platform for toxicity evaluation of environmental pollutants. This review aims to summarize the core principles of this technology, its current application status in modelling pollutant exposure and toxic responses, and to analyze its advantages including biomimetic modeling and real-time monitoring over conventional in vitro models, as well as the challenges currently faced involving chip standardization, operational complexity, and subsystem integration. The article focuses on reviewing the latest research progress of microfluidic lung on a chip in assessing the inflammation and toxicity of atmospheric particulate matter and pathogen, volatile organic compounds and aromatic hydrocarbon, and emerging micro/nanomaterials, and further envisions its broad application prospects in advancing studies in environmental toxicology, precision risk assessment, and personalized health prediction.
title: Microfluidic lung-on-a-chip for evaluating inflammation and toxicity from environmental pollutants

text: Environmental pollutants pose a global public health threat, with the respiratory system as a primary target of exposure. Pollutants such as fine particulate matter (PM), which can penetrate deep into the alveoli and induce oxidative stress, significantly increase the risk of respiratory and cardiovascular diseases (Wang et al., 2025). Microplastics and nanoplastics have emerged as ubiquitous environmental pollutants in recent years, with their detection frequently documented across a range of environmental media (Winiarska et al., 2024). These particles can enter the human body via inhalation, thereby exacerbating the health risks (Uchmanowicz et al., 2025). Such pollutants including PM2.5, ozone, nanomaterials, and various chemical substances can elicit a range of toxic effects in lung tissue, such as inflammation, oxidative stress, and barrier dysfunction (Guerra-Flórez et al., 2023). However, conventional toxicity assessment models, including animal experiments and static two-dimensional (2D) cell cultures, suffer from significant limitations. Animal models exhibit species differences that preclude accurate prediction of human physiological responses, while static 2D cell cultures fail to recapitulate the complex three-dimensional (3D) tissue architecture, cell–cell interactions, and critical physiological microenvironment (e.g., fluid condition,
title: Microfluidic lung-on-a-chip for evaluating inflammation and toxicity from environmental pollutants

text: preclude accurate prediction of human physiological responses, while static 2D cell cultures fail to recapitulate the complex three-dimensional (3D) tissue architecture, cell–cell interactions, and critical physiological microenvironment (e.g., fluid condition, air–liquid interface, and respiration-related mechanical strain) present in vivo, resulting in low throughput and poor clinical relevance (Sun et al., 2021; Irrechukwu et al., 2023). To overcome these challenges, microfluidic lung-on-a-chip technology has emerged (Huh et al., 2010; Ringquist et al., 2026). This technology integrates microfluidics, cell biology, and tissue engineering, enabling precise control over hydrodynamics, mechanical forces (e.g., cyclic stretching that mimics respiration), and co-culture of multiple cell types on a microscale chip, thereby constructing 3D lung tissue models with high physiological relevance (Wu et al., 2025). For instance, a lung-on-a-chip based on a biomimetic hydrogel membrane better recapitulates the composition and mechanical properties of the alveolar basement membrane and successfully reconstructs the alveolar–capillary barrier function (Shen et al., 2023). This platform offers an unprecedented tool for understanding the interactions between pollutants and lung tissue under dynamic conditions. In recent years, microfluidic lung-on-a-chip devices (Table 1) have been widely employed to simulate inhalation exposure to various environmental pollutants and to investigate their toxicity pathways. Of particular note, this technology has shown great potential in elucidating the pulmonary toxicity mechanisms of emerging pollutants such as nanoplastics. Research indicates that, compared with micro-/nanoplastics derived from polypropylene or polyethylene terephthalate, polystyrene particles cause the most severe impairment to the biophysical function of pulmonary surfactant; the heterogeneous aggregates they form further exacerbate lung injury at the alveolar–capillary interface (Xu et al., 2023). The organ-on-a-chip platforms for micro/nanoplastic toxicology has been reviewed too (Abdessalam et al., 2025). text: The key components of lung-on-a-chip are designed to precisely recapitulate the complex physiological microenvironment of the human lung. The chip architecture generally comprises interconnected microchannels/chambers and a porous membrane (Figure 1A) that separates an air chamber from a liquid chamber, thereby reconstituting the alveolar–capillary barrier, being a key physiological structure in vitro (Huh et al., 2010). These chips are typically fabricated from materials with good biocompatibility and optical transparency, such as polydimethylsiloxane (PDMS), using soft lithography (Yang et al., 2020). Compared with other chip materials like glass and polymethyl methacrylate, PDMS is widely used in lung-on-a-chip fabrication, owing to its biocompatibility, gas permeability, optical transparency, chemical inertness, molding convenience, and cost-effectiveness. The porous polycarbonate membrane, polycaprolactone and collagen nanofiber, and Matrigel are typically employed for constructing the biomimetic basement membrane (Zhang et al., 2020; Kanabekova et al., 2024). To more faithfully mimic the sac-like morphology of alveoli, some studies have developed a soap-bubble-inspired vesicular hydrogel membrane, which can stably withstand respiration-like cyclic mechanical stretching and fluid flow, providing a critical platform for constructing a more biomimetic alveolar–capillary barrier (She et
title: Microfluidic lung-on-a-chip for evaluating inflammation and toxicity from environmental pollutants

text: developed a soap-bubble-inspired vesicular hydrogel membrane, which can stably withstand respiration-like cyclic mechanical stretching and fluid flow, providing a critical platform for constructing a more biomimetic alveolar–capillary barrier (She et al., 2024). In terms of mechanical and hydrodynamic control, micropumps and precision pressure control systems are employed to accurately simulate respiration-like cyclic mechanical strain (typically 10% at 0.2 Hz in human alveoli) and capillary blood flow profile (e.g., 1 mm/s). As a representative condition, a flow rate of less than 1 μL/min was chosen to apply a physiologically relevant fluid shear stress (∼1 dyne/cm2) for biomimetic reconstruction (Huh et al., 2012; Li et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2020). These physical stimuli are essential for maintaining the normal phenotype and function of alveolar epithelial cells and endothelial cells (Huh et al., 2010; Koornneef et al., 2025). Cell co-culture systems form the basis for model functionalization, typically involving co-culture of human-derived alveolar epithelial cells (e.g., A549 cells, primary cells, and induced pluripotent stem cell-derived cells) with human vascular endothelial cells at an air–liquid interface (Kim et al., 2023). To construct more
title: Microfluidic lung-on-a-chip for evaluating inflammation and toxicity from environmental pollutants

text: alveolar epithelial cells (e.g., A549 cells, primary cells, and induced pluripotent stem cell-derived cells) with human vascular endothelial cells at an air–liquid interface (Kim et al., 2023). To construct more complex microphysiological systems, researchers have also introduced immune cells (e.g., macrophages) and fibroblasts into the models to mimic key cell–cell interactions and immune responses within the pulmonary microenvironment (Chen et al., 2023). In the pulmonary microenvironment, the alveolar epithelial cells closely interact with resident alveolar macrophages. Airborne pollutant exposure disrupts pulmonary immune homeostasis via oxidative stress-driven activation of epithelial–macrophage crosstalk (Dubey et al., 2026). Alarmins released from injured epithelia promote M1 macrophage polarization through NF-κB/NLRP3 signaling, releasing pro-inflammatory cytokines that recruit neutrophils and damage the epithelial barrier. Persistent imbalance between M1 and M2 macrophage responses culminates in chronic inflammation and fibrosis. Lung-on-a-chip platforms, incorporating cyclic stretch and air–liquid interface, enable physiologically relevant investigation of these dynamic immunotoxicological mechanisms. Typically, an aerosol delivery system is applied for on-chip pollutant exposure. The system mainly consists of a pollutant storage container and either a vacuum-operated inhalation simulator or a stepper-motor-driven microrespirator (Benam et

text: Functionalization of the lung-on-a-chip model must be validated through a series of quantitative endpoints to ensure its reliability in mimicking pulmonary physiological and pathological processes. Assessment of barrier function is central to validating alveolar–capillary integrity, typically accomplished by measuring transepithelial electrical resistance and performing fluorescent tracer permeability assays (Meghani et al., 2020). These methods enable quantitative evaluation of changes in barrier permeability following exposure to environmental pollutants (e.g., PM), thereby reflecting early structural damage to lung tissue induced by such pollutants (Koornneef et al., 2025). For the simulation of metabolic and clearance functions, advanced lung-on-a-chip models aim to incorporate metabolic activities such as cytochrome P450 enzymes to assess the biotransformation of pollutants within the lung (Yang et al., 2021). Meanwhile, by modelling mucociliary clearance, the deposition and clearance kinetics of airborne particles can be investigated (Yang et al., 2020). To achieve multi-parameter dynamic monitoring, lung-on-a-chip devices are often coupled with online or offline high-sensitivity detection systems. For instance, integration of real-time fluorescence microscopy, enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay, and mass spectrometry allows continuous monitoring of cell viability, secretion of inflammatory cytokines (e.g.,
title: Microfluidic lung-on-a-chip for evaluating inflammation and toxicity from environmental pollutants

text: online or offline high-sensitivity detection systems. For instance, integration of real-time fluorescence microscopy, enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay, and mass spectrometry allows continuous monitoring of cell viability, secretion of inflammatory cytokines (e.g., IL-6, IL-8), oxidative stress markers, and genomic/proteomic alterations following pollutant exposure (Chen et al., 2023; Liu et al., 2024). In addition, some studies have integrated flexible inkjet-printed pH sensors into the lung-on-a-chip for real-time monitoring of pH fluctuations in the simulated alveolar microenvironment, thereby providing a new tool for studying pollutant-induced chemical changes in the local milieu (Boček et al., 2026). Collectively, these comprehensive validation endpoints ensure that the lung-on-a-chip model possesses high physiological relevance and predictive value in environmental toxicology research.
